transcript:
HEADER: 2026-03-25 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~78m | Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Anita (Redwood Perf), Lena (Aureus ML Infra), Dmitri (Aureus SRE), Priya (Aureus MLOps), Tom (Aureus HW)

SUMMARY (auto): chasing cudagraph-induced tail-regressions on on-prem; NUMA and quantization suspected; kernel routing differences between TRT-LLM and vLLM noted.

[00:00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call, can you hear me?
[00:00:05] Lena: yeah loud and clear, thanks for doing this.
[00:00:09] Marco: all good here, wanted to set the goal—reproduce the cudagraph regression and figure out whether it is kernel scheduling, NUMA, or quantization interaction.
[00:00:20] Dmitri: our CI started seeing a 30-60ms tail bump after a driver update and some firmware. It only hits when we capture and replay graphs across mixed batch sizes.
[00:00:30] Anita: ok that pattern smells like capture-replay mismatch when tensors cross NUMA boundaries or when non-deterministic kernel selection happens at runtime.

[00:02:12] Priya: short context — we run 4xA100 per node, NVLink fully connected, but it's a 2-socket machine and Linux sometimes puts host buffers on the far node. We do Kubernetes + CRI-O.
[00:02:35] Tom: we also recently flipped BIOS interleaving settings to performance, could be related.

[00:04:00] Marco: first bench we need: pin process and CUDA allocations to the same NUMA zone during cudagraph capture and replay. If the capture allocates on socket 0 but replay lands some work on socket 1, CUDA may pick a different kernel path.
[00:04:28] Lena: how would that change kernel selection? I thought kernels are chosen by size and dtype.
[00:04:35] Marco: yes but also workspace placement and memory async copies can change whether fused kernels are viable. Example: flash-attention fused path requires specific alignment and contiguous layout; if memory is paged or remote, we fall back to a less efficient kernel or introduce extra memcpy.

[00:06:10] Anita: we also saw cases where TRT-LLM chooses persistent kernels when batch==1 steady state, but vLLM continuous-batching prefers different kernels optimized for token streams. That leads to different warmup behavior and KV cache touch patterns.
[00:06:45] Dmitri: interesting — in our runs TRT-LLM seemed stable but we saw larger variance with our custom vLLM-based runtime.

[00:09:00] Sofia: can you describe the exact failure mode again? Is it reproducible with synthetic payloads?
[00:09:07] Priya: partly. If we run uniform batch-size capture->replay it's fine. When we mix batch sizes (1,4,8) in production traffic we sometimes see a tail spike at the start of an epoch after a deployment.
[00:09:26] Marco: that points to graph cache being invalid from varying shapes forcing the runtime to recompile or select a fallback. CUDA Graph capture works best when shapes are stable; variable sequences cause multiple graphs and possible oddities when kernels are cached per-graph.

[00:11:10] Tom: also, we saw page faults reported during replay in Linux dmesg. Could that be NUMA thrashing?
[00:11:22] Anita: yep page faults indicate memory migrations. If the page migrates the GPU kernel may stall waiting on host->device pin or driver-level work. That will amplify tail latency.

[00:13:45] Marco: two experiments: 1) force NUMA-local allocation with numactl --cpunodebind/--membind and use CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping to align GPU to CPU. 2) disable CUDA Graph and run dynamic batching to compare tail.

[00:15:30] Lena: will disabling cudagraph reduce throughput? we need the perf for cost targets.
[00:15:37] Marco: potentially yes, but the question is delta: if cudagraph gives average token throughput +8% but introduces 50ms tail spikes, for user-facing latencies that might be unacceptable. We need to measure p50/p95/p99.

[00:17:02] Dmitri: one of our patches was changing cgroup mem limits which might make allocations fall back to swap or cause kernel to fall back to a different allocator in the CUDA driver.
[00:17:20] Anita: swap + GPU is a no-go — any involvement of swap will blow up tail latency. Make sure vm.swappiness and cgroup limits aren't causing anonymous pages to migrate.

[00:19:10] Marco: let's talk quantization. We saw the regression is slightly larger with int8 profiles. Is it possible that int8 kernels pick different operator fusions that are fragile?
[00:19:30] Priya: yes, we tried GPTQ for some models — the int8 path used a per-tile fused matmul+dequant kernel in TRT-LLM and that path requires a contiguous layout. If KV cache fragmentation occurs, the fused path can't be used.

[00:21:00] Sofia: are there known differences in kernel selection between TRT-LLM and vLLM that we should expect?
[00:21:12] Marco: summary: TRT-LLM heavily leverages cuBLAS/cudNN+TensorRT graph optimizations and will pick persistent/prefetch kernels assuming steady shapes. vLLM tends to prefer small-kernel, low-latency ops and dynamic batching strategies. TRT-LLM's persistent kernels are sensitive to workspace placement and can be brittle if memory margins are tight. vLLM may avoid some fused kernels and instead use many smaller kernels which can be more robust but cost more aggregate time unless the runtime batches well.

[00:23:05] Tom: we observed that after a CUDA driver update, TRT-LLM persistent kernel path sometimes falls back to a generic matmul when cuBLAS algorithm heuristics change. That could match our timing of regression.

[00:24:40] Marco: ok then two-pronged approach: reproduce with the exact driver + firmware combo in your lab, and run both TRT-LLM and vLLM on identical pinned NUMA allocations. Capture kernel selection trace (cuBLAS algorithm chosen, kernels fused, workspace sizes).

[00:26:58] Anita: also instrument KV cache behavior: when using persistent attention or prefix caching, eviction pattern matters. If the KV store is fragmented across NUMA or if prefetching is not aligning to GPU prefetch windows, you'll see token stalls.

[00:28:10] Priya: can you explain the eviction/prefetch interplay? We're using a simple LRU per-shard cache.
[00:28:20] Marco: LRU per-shard is ok but if the cache eviction causes KV pages to be freed and reallocated on a different NUMA node, the next touch will trigger remote access. For GPUs, remote host memory means extra latency in H2D copies or page migration. Prefetch windows that align eviction with upcoming requests reduce this. A predictive prefetch tied to request routing reduces misses.

[00:30:00] Sofia: is Redwood's runtime doing any NUMA-aware allocation or is that left to the OS?
[00:30:06] Marco: Redwood's on-prem agent has an option to pin allocations per-GPU and to use libcudart with hostAlloc flags to prefer pinned host memory on the right NUMA node. But we also rely on customer orchestration to keep containers pinned. We recommended numactl and strict node affinity for on-prem.

[00:32:55] Dmitri: what about MIG or partitioning? We're considering MIG on A100 to host mixed workloads. Could that change kernel selection?
[00:33:10] Anita: MIG changes resource visibility and tile sizes; it could prevent persistent kernels that expect full GPU workspace. Many fused kernels assume large contiguous memory; MIG may force smaller workspaces and cause kernel graph to choose a different algorithm.

[00:34:55] Marco: now let's talk about debugging: collect the following traces — nvprof/ncu for kernels, cuBLAS algorithm logs, dmesg for page faults, process NUMA maps (numactl --hardware + /proc/<pid>/numa_maps), and CUDA IPC/pinned allocations stats.

[00:36:20] Priya: ok we can collect; how do we correlate kernel selection to cudagraph replay?
[00:36:32] Marco: capture at two points: 1) during capture (when the graph was recorded) collect kernel list and workspace sizes; 2) during replay collect chosen kernels and any fallback to generic algorithms. Differences point to selection nondeterminism.

[00:38:40] Lena: anything else with quant that we should watch? per-channel scale vs per-tensor scale?
[00:38:48] Anita: per-channel quant is more accurate but requires different dequant kernels with additional memory and compute. Some fused int8 kernels assume per-tensor scales for simpler packing; if you switch to per-channel, you may fall back to slower code paths. Also asymmetric vs symmetric quant affects clip/zero-point handling which changes kernel math and can force different operator registrations in TRT-LLM.

[00:40:12] Marco: practical advice: run int8 microbenchmarks with both per-tensor and per-channel settings, and capture which kernels are used. We saw up to 20% perf delta simply from that choice.

[00:42:05] Dmitri: about cudagraphs — we use multiple graphs for different prompt lengths. Is it better to compile a superset graph?
[00:42:16] Marco: superset graphs can work but increase workspace and maybe not fit memory causing swaps. Another pattern is lightweight dynamic graphs with small capture windows; but that loses some cudagraph speed. For on-prem, we prefer deterministic shape buckets (1,8,32) and route requests accordingly.

[00:44:30] Priya: what about tail latency mitigation—fallback to smaller models or degraded modes?
[00:44:39] Sofia: Redwood has policy routing to fallback to a cheaper model variant or to warm-start KV cache with a low-quality fast path. We can also prefer vLLM path when traffic is bursty since it's better at dynamic batching.

[00:46:55] Anita: a trick: during a rollout, keep the old runtime available as a canary for cold-start traffic, route 5% and compare p99. Also warm the cache with synthetic prompts.

[00:48:20] Tom: on the hardware side we'll verify BIOS interleaving and set IOMMU passthrough consistent. We'll also lock CPU governors to performance.

[00:49:55] Marco: let's lock down the exact bench plan — Marco will provide a microbenchmark script that runs: shape-buckets, cudagraph capture+replay, int8/per-channel/per-tensor, pinned NUMA, and logs cuBLAS picks.

[00:50:12] Sofia: I'll send our secure runner (container) and the SOC2/ISO compliance package so you can sign the NDA and run tests in your lab.

[00:51:30] Dmitri: quick aside — how do we measure KV cache fragmentation? any tooling?
[00:51:40] Marco: we instrument the KV allocator to report contiguous runs, fragmentation ratio, and percent remote pages. We'll add instrumentation to the sample runner.

[00:53:05] Lena: what about driver rollback? Is that an acceptable mitigation?
[00:53:12] Anita: yes, if we identify a specific driver version that regresses. But we should prefer to understand cause because driver rollbacks aren't always allowed in prod. Also coordinate with firmware and CUDA toolkit pairings; mismatch often causes surprises.

[00:55:00] Priya: any red flags with KMS or VPC for on-prem? We're worried about key access and throughput if we integrate HSM for model encryption.
[00:55:10] Sofia: Redwood supports local KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys. The main perf risk is if decryption is done synchronously on-request; we recommend decrypt-on-launch and keep keys in a cached, ephemeral in-memory store with strict TTLs. We'll share our KMS integration guide.

[00:57:22] Tom: are there any known regression patches in TRT-LLM around cudagraph?
[00:57:30] Marco: TRT-LLM had a change in their graph executor heuristics that landed in late 2025 which affected algorithm selection heuristics for small-batch fused kernels. We can cross-reference release notes but best to validate with their repro too.

[00:59:08] Anita: for measurements, collect p50/p90/p95/p99, and also kernel-level histograms. We'll correlate p99 spikes to specific kernels or page faults.

[01:01:20] Marco: one more note — if you use transparent huge pages (THP) it can change allocation patterns. We usually recommend disabling THP for consistent NUMA-aware allocations.

[01:02:36] Dmitri: good to know. We'll check sysctl vm.nr_hugepages and thp status.

[01:04:10] Sofia: recap of next steps — Marco share microbench, Dmitri provision pinned NUMA lab and run with given driver, Sofia send compliance and runner, Anita will add KV fragmentation instrumentation, and we'll meet in two weeks for results.

[01:04:45] Lena: thanks everyone, this was useful — appreciate the concrete steps.
[01:05:00] Sofia: thanks all, we'll follow up in calendar and I'll attach the runner repo.

END TRANSCRIPT
